claim: TMC proteins are a highly conserved ion channel family consisting of eight members (TMC1–TMC8) in mammals.
source: Transmembrane channel-like (TMC) proteins are a highly conserved ion channel family consisting of eight members (TMC1–TMC8) in mammals.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TMC protein family composition in mammals.

claim: TMC1/2 are components of the mechanotransduction channel in hair cells.
source: TMC1/2 are components of the mechanotransduction channel in hair cells, and mutations of TMC1/2 cause deafness in humans and mice.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about TMC1/2 function, supported by prior research.

claim: Mutations of TMC1/2 cause deafness in humans and mice.
source: TMC1/2 are components of the mechanotransduction channel in hair cells, and mutations of TMC1/2 cause deafness in humans and mice.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the consequences of TMC1/2 mutations.

claim: Tmc7 is specifically expressed in the testis.
source: Here, we show that Tmc7 is specifically expressed in the testis and that it is required for acrosome biogenesis during spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by expression analysis data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Tmc7 is required for acrosome biogenesis during spermatogenesis.
source: Here, we show that Tmc7 is specifically expressed in the testis and that it is required for acrosome biogenesis during spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by knockout mouse phenotype data.

claim: Tmc7−/− mice exhibited abnormal sperm head.
source: Tmc7−/− mice exhibited abnormal sperm head, disorganized mitochondrial sheaths, and reduced number of elongating spermatids, similar to human oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by morphological analysis data in Figure 2.

claim: Tmc7−/− mice exhibited disorganized mitochondrial sheaths.
source: Tmc7−/− mice exhibited abnormal sperm head, disorganized mitochondrial sheaths, and reduced number of elongating spermatids, similar to human oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Mito-tracker staining data in Figure 2H.

claim: Tmc7−/− mice exhibited reduced number of elongating spermatids.
source: Tmc7−/− mice exhibited abnormal sperm head, disorganized mitochondrial sheaths, and reduced number of elongating spermatids, similar to human oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological analysis data in Figure 2.

claim: Tmc7−/− mice phenotype is similar to human oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia.
source: Tmc7−/− mice exhibited abnormal sperm head, disorganized mitochondrial sheaths, and reduced number of elongating spermatids, similar to human oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotypic similarities between the mouse model and human condition.

claim: TMC7 is colocalized with GM130 at the cis-Golgi region in round spermatids.
source: We further demonstrate that TMC7 is colocalized with GM130 at the cis-Golgi region in round spermatids.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence co-staining data in Figure 4B.

claim: TMC7 deficiency leads to aberrant Golgi morphology.
source: TMC7 deficiency leads to aberrant Golgi morphology and impaired fusion of Golgi-derived vesicles to the developing acrosome.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TEM and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3.

claim: TMC7 deficiency leads to impaired fusion of Golgi-derived vesicles to the developing acrosome.
source: TMC7 deficiency leads to aberrant Golgi morphology and impaired fusion of Golgi-derived vesicles to the developing acrosome.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TEM showing accumulated vesicles and GOPC/PNA colocalization data in Figure 3.

claim: Upon loss of TMC7, intracellular ion homeostasis is impaired.
source: Moreover, upon loss of TMC7 intracellular ion homeostasis is impaired and ROS levels are increased, which in turn causes Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum stress.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry measurements of Ca2+ and pH in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Upon loss of TMC7, ROS levels are increased.
source: Moreover, upon loss of TMC7 intracellular ion homeostasis is impaired and ROS levels are increased, which in turn causes Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum stress.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry measurements in Figure 5C.

claim: Increased ROS levels upon loss of TMC7 cause Golgi stress.
source: Moreover, upon loss of TMC7 intracellular ion homeostasis is impaired and ROS levels are increased, which in turn causes Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed increase in Golgi stress markers (HSP47, TFE3) shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Increased ROS levels upon loss of TMC7 cause endoplasmic reticulum stress.
source: Moreover, upon loss of TMC7 intracellular ion homeostasis is impaired and ROS levels are increased, which in turn causes Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed increase in ER stress markers (p-EIF2α, CHOP, GRP78) shown in Figure 5D.

claim: TMC7 is required to maintain pH and ion homeostasis, which is needed for acrosome biogenesis.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that TMC7 is required to maintain pH and ion homeostasis, which is needed for acrosome biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the combined data showing disrupted pH/ion homeostasis and acrosome defects.

claim: Spermiogenesis is the post-meiotic phase of male germ cell development during which the haploid spermatids differentiate into mature spermatozoa.
source: Spermiogenesis is the post-meiotic phase of male germ cell development during which the haploid spermatids differentiate into mature spermatozoa (Kang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mouse spermiogenesis consists of 16 steps characterized by morphological changes in acrosome formation, nuclear condensation and elongation, flagellum formation, and cytoplasm removal.
source: Mouse spermiogenesis consists of 16 steps characterized by morphological changes in acrosome formation, nuclear condensation and elongation, flagellum formation, and cytoplasm removal (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Acrosome biogenesis is one of the key events of spermiogenesis.
source: Acrosome biogenesis is one of the key events of spermiogenesis, and it begins with the initial stage of spermatid development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about spermiogenesis.

claim: Acrosome biogenesis begins with the initial stage of spermatid development.
source: Acrosome biogenesis is one of the key events of spermiogenesis, and it begins with the initial stage of spermatid development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the timing of acrosome biogenesis.

claim: The acrosome is a specialized organelle with a cap-like structure covering the anterior part of the mature spermatozoon head.
source: The acrosome is a specialized organelle with a cap-like structure covering the anterior part of the mature spermatozoon head and is indispensable for the fertilization process (Xiong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about acrosome structure supported by citation.

claim: The acrosome is indispensable for the fertilization process.
source: The acrosome is a specialized organelle with a cap-like structure covering the anterior part of the mature spermatozoon head and is indispensable for the fertilization process (Xiong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about acrosome function supported by citation.

claim: Acrosome biogenesis is thought to be derived from the Golgi complex in early spermatids.
source: Although acrosome biogenesis is thought to be derived from the Golgi complex in early spermatids, growing evidence suggests that the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and lysosomes are involved in acrosome biogenesis (Khawar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Growing evidence suggests that the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and lysosomes are involved in acrosome biogenesis.
source: Although acrosome biogenesis is thought to be derived from the Golgi complex in early spermatids, growing evidence suggests that the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and lysosomes are involved in acrosome biogenesis (Khawar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Defects in acrosome biogenesis can result in subfertility or infertility.
source: Defects in acrosome biogenesis can result in subfertility or infertility.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the consequences of acrosome defects.

claim: Acrosome biogenesis is generally classified into four successive phases, namely the Golgi, cap, acrosome, and maturation phases.
source: Acrosome biogenesis is generally classified into four successive phases, namely the Golgi, cap, acrosome, and maturation phases (Xu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HSP90B1 is an ER molecular chaperone that has been shown to be a testis-specific protein.
source: Heat shock protein 90B1 (HSP90B1) is an ER molecular chaperone that has been shown to be a testis-specific protein, and HSP90B1 deficiency leads to a globozoospermia-syndrome like phenotype (Audouard and Christians, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HSP90B1 deficiency leads to a globozoospermia-syndrome like phenotype.
source: Heat shock protein 90B1 (HSP90B1) is an ER molecular chaperone that has been shown to be a testis-specific protein, and HSP90B1 deficiency leads to a globozoospermia-syndrome like phenotype (Audouard and Christians, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: GM130 localizes on the cis surface of the Golgi apparatus.
source: GM130 (Golgi matrix protein 130) localize on the cis surface of the Golgi apparatus, and loss of GM130 causes acrosome malformations and results in male infertility (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Loss of GM130 causes acrosome malformations and results in male infertility.
source: GM130 (Golgi matrix protein 130) localize on the cis surface of the Golgi apparatus, and loss of GM130 causes acrosome malformations and results in male infertility (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: GOPC is a trans-Golgi-associated protein that plays a role in vesicle transport from the Golgi apparatus.
source: GOPC (Golgi-associated PDZ and coiled-coil motif-containing) is a trans-Golgi-associated protein that plays a role in vesicle transport from the Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GOPC function.

claim: GOPC deficiency leads to vesicle transport failure, which in turn results in malformation of the acrosome and to infertility.
source: GOPC deficiency leads to vesicle transport failure, which in turn results in malformation of the acrosome and to infertility (Yao et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: PICK1, ICA1l, and VPS13b are involved in proacrosomal vesicle trafficking during acrosome formation.
source: Other vesicle transport proteins including PICK1, ICA1l, and VPS13b are involved in proacrosomal vesicle trafficking during acrosome formation (Xiao et al., 2009; He et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Autophagy is involved in proacrosomal vesicle fusion and transport to form the acrosome.
source: Recent evidence suggests that autophagy is involved in proacrosomal vesicle fusion and transport to form the acrosome, and disruption of ATG7 (Wang et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2021) or ATG5 causes aberrant acrosome formation and male infertility or subfertility.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Disruption of ATG7 causes aberrant acrosome formation and male infertility or subfertility.
source: Recent evidence suggests that autophagy is involved in proacrosomal vesicle fusion and transport to form the acrosome, and disruption of ATG7 (Wang et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2021) or ATG5 causes aberrant acrosome formation and male infertility or subfertility.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Disruption of ATG5 causes aberrant acrosome formation and male infertility or subfertility.
source: Recent evidence suggests that autophagy is involved in proacrosomal vesicle fusion and transport to form the acrosome, and disruption of ATG7 (Wang et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2021) or ATG5 causes aberrant acrosome formation and male infertility or subfertility.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (implied).

claim: Eight TMC family members (TMC1–TMC8) are identified in humans and mice.
source: Transmembrane channel-like (TMC) proteins are highly conserved ion channel-like proteins, with eight family members (TMC1–TMC8) identified in humans and mice (Keresztes et al., 2003; Kurima et al., 2003; Yue et al., 2019; Kurima et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TMC proteins are predicted to have 6–10 transmembrane domains.
source: TMC proteins are predicted to have 6–10 transmembrane domains, and all protein members contain a conserved 120 amino acid TMC domain (Yue et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: All TMC protein members contain a conserved 120 amino acid TMC domain.
source: TMC proteins are predicted to have 6–10 transmembrane domains, and all protein members contain a conserved 120 amino acid TMC domain (Yue et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TMC1 assembles as dimers.
source: The single-particle cryo-electron microscopy structure shows that TMC1 assembles as dimers and that each monomer contains 10 transmembrane domains with four domains (S4–S7) that line the channel pore (Jeong et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Each TMC1 monomer contains 10 transmembrane domains with four domains (S4–S7) that line the channel pore.
source: The single-particle cryo-electron microscopy structure shows that TMC1 assembles as dimers and that each monomer contains 10 transmembrane domains with four domains (S4–S7) that line the channel pore (Jeong et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Tmc1 and Tmc2 are mechano-electrical transducer (MET) channels in cochlear hair cells.
source: Tmc1 and 2 are mechano-electrical transducer (MET) channels in cochlear hair cells, and mutations in Tmc1/2 cause deafness in humans and mice (Nist-Lund et al., 2019a) by disrupting hair cell mechanoelectrical transduction, and Tmc gene therapy can restore auditory function and balance in mice (Askew et al., 2015; Nist-Lund et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mutations in Tmc1/2 cause deafness in humans and mice by disrupting hair cell mechanoelectrical transduction.
source: Tmc1 and 2 are mechano-electrical transducer (MET) channels in cochlear hair cells, and mutations in Tmc1/2 cause deafness in humans and mice (Nist-Lund et al., 2019a) by disrupting hair cell mechanoelectrical transduction, and Tmc gene therapy can restore auditory function and balance in mice (Askew et al., 2015; Nist-Lund et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Tmc gene therapy can restore auditory function and balance in mice.
source: Tmc1 and 2 are mechano-electrical transducer (MET) channels in cochlear hair cells, and mutations in Tmc1/2 cause deafness in humans and mice (Nist-Lund et al., 2019a) by disrupting hair cell mechanoelectrical transduction, and Tmc gene therapy can restore auditory function and balance in mice (Askew et al., 2015; Nist-Lund et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Germline mutations in Tmc6 and Tmc8 are associated with epidermodysplasia verruciformis.
source: Germline mutations in Tmc6 and Tmc8 are associated with epidermodysplasia verruciformis, which leads to increased susceptibility to human papilloma virus (HPV) infection (Kurima et al., 2003; Yue et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Epidermodysplasia verruciformis leads to increased susceptibility to human papilloma virus (HPV) infection.
source: Germline mutations in Tmc6 and Tmc8 are associated with epidermodysplasia verruciformis, which leads to increased susceptibility to human papilloma virus (HPV) infection (Kurima et al., 2003; Yue et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Only Tmc5 and Tmc7 exhibited elevated expression in the testis during development among the eight Tmc family members.
source: Among the eight Tmc family members, we found that only Tmc5 and Tmc7 exhibited elevated expression in the testis during development (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by analysis of developmental transcriptome data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Tmc7 was expressed at higher levels than Tmc5 in the testis during development.
source: Tmc7 caught our great interest because Tmc7 was expressed at higher levels than Tmc5 in the testis during development.
evidence: This is inferred from the transcriptome data analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Tmc7 was predominantly expressed in the testis compared with all other analyzed tissues.
source: We found that Tmc7 was predominantly expressed in the testis compared with all other analyzed tissues (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-cell transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tmc7 began to be expressed in diplotene spermatocytes in mouse testes.
source: Interestingly, Tmc7 began to be expressed in diplotene spermatocytes and was expressed at high levels in round spermatids in mouse testes (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-cell sequencing data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Tmc7 was expressed at high levels in round spermatids in mouse testes.
source: Interestingly, Tmc7 began to be expressed in diplotene spermatocytes and was expressed at high levels in round spermatids in mouse testes (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-cell sequencing data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The Tmc7 expression pattern was confirmed by RT-PCR.
source: The Tmc7 expression pattern was confirmed by RT-PCR (Figure 1E and F), and Tmc7 was again found to be highly expressed in round spermatids of human testis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Tmc7 was highly expressed in round spermatids of human testis.
source: The Tmc7 expression pattern was confirmed by RT-PCR (Figure 1E and F), and Tmc7 was again found to be highly expressed in round spermatids of human testis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-cell sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tmc7–/– mice were viable.
source: We then examined the phenotypes and found that Tmc7–/– mice were viable and had a normal appearance and exhibited a normal metabolic rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from phenotypic observation of knockout mice.

claim: Tmc7–/– mice had a normal appearance.
source: We then examined the phenotypes and found that Tmc7–/– mice were viable and had a normal appearance and exhibited a normal metabolic rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from phenotypic observation of knockout mice.

claim: Tmc7–/– mice exhibited a normal metabolic rate.
source: We then examined the phenotypes and found that Tmc7–/– mice were viable and had a normal appearance and exhibited a normal metabolic rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by metabolic cage measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tmc7–/– male mice exhibited complete infertility.
source: Moreover, Tmc7–/– male mice exhibited complete infertility (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by fertility testing data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: There was no difference in the number of tubules per testicle between Tmc7−/− and WT mice.
source: No difference in the number of tubules per testicle or in the number of Sertoli cells was seen when comparing Tmc7−/− and WT mice; Sertoli cell were identified by immunofluorescence staining of the Sertoli cell marker SOX9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no difference in the number of Sertoli cells between Tmc7−/− and WT mice.
source: No difference in the number of tubules per testicle or in the number of Sertoli cells was seen when comparing Tmc7−/− and WT mice; Sertoli cell were identified by immunofluorescence staining of the Sertoli cell marker SOX9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The populations of germ cells were comparable between wild type (WT) and Tmc7–/– mice at postnatal day (PD)14 and PD21.
source: In seminiferous tubules, the populations of germ cells were comparable between wild type (WT) and Tmc7–/– mice at postnatal day (PD)14 and PD21.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological analysis at different developmental stages.

claim: The number of elongating spermatids in Tmc7–/– mice decreased significantly compared with WT mice at PD28.
source: Intriguingly, the number of elongating spermatids in Tmc7–/– mice decreased significantly compared with WT mice at PD28 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spermiogenesis defects were observed in Tmc7–/– mice as evidenced by the reduced number of elongating spermatids.
source: We observed spermiogenesis defects in Tmc7–/– mice as evidenced by the reduced number of elongating spermatids, the increased number of sloughed germ cells, and large vacuoles in the seminiferous tubules and cauda epididymis (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Spermiogenesis defects were observed in Tmc7–/– mice as evidenced by the increased number of sloughed germ cells.
source: We observed spermiogenesis defects in Tmc7–/– mice as evidenced by the reduced number of elongating spermatids, the increased number of sloughed germ cells, and large vacuoles in the seminiferous tubules and cauda epididymis (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Spermiogenesis defects were observed in Tmc7–/– mice as evidenced by large vacuoles in the seminiferous tubules and cauda epididymis.
source: We observed spermiogenesis defects in Tmc7–/– mice as evidenced by the reduced number of elongating spermatids, the increased number of sloughed germ cells, and large vacuoles in the seminiferous tubules and cauda epididymis (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The vacuolation became more serious with increasing age in Tmc7–/– mice.
source: The vacuolation became more serious with increasing age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological analysis at different ages shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The total number of sperm in the cauda epididymis was drastically decreased in Tmc7–/– mice (~0.15 × 106 cells) compared to WT mice (~8.0 × 106 cells).
source: The total number of sperm in the cauda epididymis was drastically decreased in Tmc7–/– mice (~0.15 × 106 cells) compared to WT mice (~8.0 × 106 cells) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sperm counting data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A large proportion of spermatozoa (~70%) in Tmc7–/– mice exhibited abnormal head morphology.
source: The morphological assessment of spermatozoa from the caudal epididymis revealed that a large proportion of spermatozoa (~70%) in Tmc7–/– mice exhibited abnormal head morphology, similar to human OAT (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: A large number of spermatids failed to differentiate into elongated spermatids with sickle-shaped heads and instead exhibited abnormal head morphology in Tmc7–/– mice.
source: In parallel with this, periodic acid Schiff (PAS) staining indicated that a large number of spermatids failed to differentiate into elongated spermatids with sickle-shaped heads and instead exhibited abnormal head morphology.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by PAS staining analysis.

claim: The total number of spermatids began to significantly decrease at steps 9–12 of spermiogenesis in Tmc7–/– mice.
source: The total number of spermatids began to significantly decrease at steps 9–12 of spermiogenesis (Figure 2F and G), and we performed Mito-tracker staining and found shortened or disorganized mitochondrial sheaths in Tmc7–/– spermatozoa collected from the cauda epididymis (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Shortened or disorganized mitochondrial sheaths were found in Tmc7–/– spermatozoa collected from the cauda epididymis.
source: The total number of spermatids began to significantly decrease at steps 9–12 of spermiogenesis (Figure 2F and G), and we performed Mito-tracker staining and found shortened or disorganized mitochondrial sheaths in Tmc7–/– spermatozoa collected from the cauda epididymis (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Mito-tracker staining shown in Figure 2H.

claim: No motile or progressive sperm were found in the Tmc7–/– mice.
source: Meanwhile, no motile or progressive sperm were found in the Tmc7–/– mice (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sperm motility analysis shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: Meiotic progression was not affected in Tmc7–/– mice.
source: Moreover, meiotic progression was not affected in Tmc7–/– mice as evidenced by immunofluorescence staining of the meiosis markers SYCP3 (red) and γH2AX (green) in the seminiferous tubules of PD20 WT and Tmc7–/– mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spermatids in Tmc7–/– mice exhibited abnormal acrosome morphology as early as the Golgi phase.
source: The spermatids of WT mice had normal structures in the Golgi, cap, acrosome, and maturation phases, while spermatids in Tmc7–/– mice exhibited abnormal acrosome morphology as early as the Golgi phase.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by PNA staining analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fragmented and malformed acrosomes were observed in all four phases of spermatids in the Tmc7–/– mice.
source: Fragmented and malformed acrosomes were observed in all four phases of spermatids in the Tmc7–/– mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by PNA staining shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Absent or fragmented acrosomes were found in Tmc7–/– spermatids collected from the cauda epididymis.
source: Absent or fragmented acrosomes were also found in Tmc7–/– spermatids collected from the cauda epididymis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by PNA staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Large vesicles accumulated adjacent to developing acrosomes in all phases of acrosome biogenesis, starting from the Golgi phase in the spermatids of Tmc7–/– mice.
source: We found that large vesicles accumulated adjacent to developing acrosomes in all phases of acrosome biogenesis, starting from the Golgi phase (Figure 3B, left panel) in the spermatids of Tmc7–/– mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TEM images shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Abnormal acrosome structures were observed in Tmc7–/– spermatids.
source: Additionally, abnormal acrosome structures and defective nuclear condensation were observed in Tmc7–/– spermatids (Figure 3B, right panels).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TEM images shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Defective nuclear condensation was observed in Tmc7–/– spermatids.
source: Additionally, abnormal acrosome structures and defective nuclear condensation were observed in Tmc7–/– spermatids (Figure 3B, right panels).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TEM images shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Knockout of Tmc7 resulted in Golgi apparatus fragmentation and disorganization.
source: Further investigation revealed that knockout of Tmc7 resulted in Golgi apparatus fragmentation and disorganization, as determined by TEM and immunofluorescence staining of the Golgi marker GM130 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TEM and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The aspect ratio (height over width) of the Golgi apparatuses in Tmc7–/– spermatids (R = ~2.9) were significantly smaller than in WT spermatids (R = ~4.9).
source: The aspect ratio (height over width) of the Golgi apparatuses in Tmc7–/– spermatids (R = ~2.9) based on TEM images were also significantly smaller than in WT spermatids (R = ~4.9) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of TEM images shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Golgi body failed to correctly orient toward the acrosome in Tmc7–/– spermatids.
source: Meanwhile, we found that the Golgi body failed to correctly orient toward the acrosome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The protein levels of HSP47 and TFE3 were significantly increased upon loss of TMC7 in 3-week-old testes.
source: The results showed that the protein levels of HSP47 and TFE3 were significantly increased upon loss of TMC7, indicating the occurrence of Golgi stress (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Increased levels of HSP47 and TFE3 indicate the occurrence of Golgi stress.
source: The results showed that the protein levels of HSP47 and TFE3 were significantly increased upon loss of TMC7, indicating the occurrence of Golgi stress (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of HSP47 and TFE3 as Golgi stress markers.

claim: GOPC is localized in the trans-Golgi network and is involved in the transport and fusion of the proacrosomal vesicles with the acrosome.
source: GOPC is localized in the trans-Golgi network and is involved in the transport and fusion of the proacrosomal vesicles with the acrosome (Yao et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: GOPC staining (red) was colocalized with PNA (green) in WT spermatids.
source: By immunostaining for GOPC and PNA, we found that GOPC staining (red) was colocalized with PNA (green) in WT spermatids.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Colocalized GOPC and PNA spermatids were significantly decreased in Tmc7–/– mice.
source: In contrast, colocalized GOPC and PNA spermatids were significantly decreased in Tmc7–/– mice (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3F.

claim: TMC7 was predominantly expressed in the perinuclear regions of pachytene spermatocytes and round spermatids in WT testes.
source: We performed immunostaining and found that TMC7 was predominantly expressed in the perinuclear regions of pachytene spermatocytes and round spermatids in WT testes but not in Tmc7–/– testes, suggesting the specificity of the antibody (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TMC7 was not expressed in Tmc7–/– testes.
source: We performed immunostaining and found that TMC7 was predominantly expressed in the perinuclear regions of pachytene spermatocytes and round spermatids in WT testes but not in Tmc7–/– testes, suggesting the specificity of the antibody (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supporting antibody specificity, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TMC7 colocalized closely with GM130.
source: By immunofluorescence co-staining of TMC7 with the cis-Golgi marker GM130, the trans-Golgi marker TGN46, and PNA, we found that TMC7 colocalized closely with GM130 but not with TGN46 (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating its localization to the cis-Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence co-staining shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TMC7 did not colocalize with TGN46.
source: By immunofluorescence co-staining of TMC7 with the cis-Golgi marker GM130, the trans-Golgi marker TGN46, and PNA, we found that TMC7 colocalized closely with GM130 but not with TGN46 (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating its localization to the cis-Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence co-staining shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TMC7 is localized to the cis-Golgi apparatus.
source: By immunofluorescence co-staining of TMC7 with the cis-Golgi marker GM130, the trans-Golgi marker TGN46, and PNA, we found that TMC7 colocalized closely with GM130 but not with TGN46 (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating its localization to the cis-Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization with GM130 (cis-Golgi marker) and lack of colocalization with TGN46 (trans-Golgi marker).

claim: TMC7 and PNA were closely associated but not colocalized.
source: Further evaluation showed that TMC7 and PNA were closely associated but not colocalized (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence co-staining shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TMC7 was able to pull down GM130, the GM130-interacting protein P115, and GRASP65.
source: In parallel, we carried out co-immunoprecipitation with TMC7 antibody coupled with immunoblotting in mouse testes and found that TMC7 was able to pull down GM130, the GM130-interacting protein P115, and GRASP65 (Figure 4E), further confirming that TMC7 is localized to the cis-Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: GM130 is involved in maintaining the function and integrity of the Golgi apparatus.
source: GM130 is reported to be involved in maintaining the function and integrity of the Golgi apparatus (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The protein levels of GM130, P115, and GRASP65 were significantly reduced in Tmc7–/– testes compared to WT testes in the same stage seminiferous tubules.
source: The results showed that in the same stage seminiferous tubules, the protein levels of GM130, P115, and GRASP65 were significantly reduced in Tmc7–/– testes compared to WT testes (Figure 4F and G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Immunoblotting verified the reduced levels of GM130, P115, and GRASP65 upon loss of TMC7 in the testes of 3- and 9-week-old mice.
source: Immunoblotting further verified the reduced levels of GM130, P115, and GRASP65 upon loss of TMC7 in the testes of 3- and 9-week-old mice (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Intracellular ion homeostasis is essential for proper function, including membrane trafficking, protein glycosylation, and protein sorting.
source: Intracellular ion homeostasis is essential for proper function, including membrane trafficking, protein glycosylation, and protein sorting (Li and Wang, 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The Golgi apparatus is an intracellular Ca2+ store in addition to the ER.
source: The Golgi apparatus has been shown to be another intracellular Ca2+ store in addition to the ER (Lissandron et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Tmc1 mutation leads to reduced Ca2+ permeability, thus triggering hair cell apoptosis and subsequent deafness.
source: Tmc1 mutation leads to reduced Ca2+ permeability, thus triggering hair cell apoptosis and subsequent deafness (Fettiplace et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The intracellular Ca2+ concentration was significantly reduced in Tmc7–/– germ cells compared to WT germ cells from PD21 testes.
source: We measured intracellular Ca2+ by flow cytometry in WT and Tmc7–/– germ cells isolated from PD21 and PD30 testes. The results showed that the intracellular Ca2+ concentration was significantly reduced in Tmc7–/– germ cells compared to WT germ cells (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Intracellular pH was increased in Tmc7–/– germ cells compared to WT germ cells.
source: In contrast, intracellular pH was increased in Tmc7–/– germ cells compared to WT germ cells (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ROS levels were significantly increased upon loss of TMC7.
source: We further measured the reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and observed that ROS levels were significantly increased upon loss of TMC7 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: p-EIF2α, CHOP, and GRP78 were significantly increased in 3- and 9-week-old Tmc7–/– testes compared with WT testes.
source: In addition, we examined ER stress-related proteins by immunoblotting and found that p-EIF2α, CHOP, and GRP78 were significantly increased in 3- and 9-week-old Tmc7–/– testes compared with WT testes, indicating the occurrence of ER stress (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Increased p-EIF2α, CHOP, and GRP78 indicate the occurrence of ER stress.
source: In addition, we examined ER stress-related proteins by immunoblotting and found that p-EIF2α, CHOP, and GRP78 were significantly increased in 3- and 9-week-old Tmc7–/– testes compared with WT testes, indicating the occurrence of ER stress (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of these proteins as ER stress markers.

claim: There was no difference in the number of TUNEL-positive cells between 3-week-old WT and Tmc7–/– mice in seminiferous tubules.
source: There was no difference in the number of TUNEL-positive cells between 3-week-old WT and Tmc7–/– mice of seminiferous tubules.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TUNEL assay data.

claim: TUNEL-positive cells in seminiferous tubules and cauda epididymis were significantly increased in 9-week-old Tmc7–/– mice compared to WT mice.
source: The TUNEL-positive cells in seminiferous tubules and cauda epididymis were significantly increased in 9-week-old Tmc7–/– mice compared to WT mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Depletion of TMC7 increased the levels of Cleaved-CASPASE-3 and BAX.
source: The expression of apoptosis-related proteins was next measured by immunoblotting in 9-week-old WT and Tmc7–/– mice, depletion of TMC7 increased the levels of Cleaved-CASPASE-3 and BAX and decreased the levels of BCL2 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Depletion of TMC7 decreased the levels of BCL2.
source: The expression of apoptosis-related proteins was next measured by immunoblotting in 9-week-old WT and Tmc7–/– mice, depletion of TMC7 increased the levels of Cleaved-CASPASE-3 and BAX and decreased the levels of BCL2 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: TMC1 and TMC2 are localized to the site of MET channels at the tips of the shorter stereocilia of cochlear hair cells.
source: Among the eight TMC protein members, TMC1 and TMC2 are localized to the site of MET channels at the tips of the shorter stereocilia of cochlear hair cells (Beurg et al., 2019; Kurima et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TMC1 and TMC2 expressed in heterologous cell lines remain in the ER and fail to localize to the plasma membrane.
source: However, TMC1 and TMC2 expressed in heterologous cell lines remain in the ER and fail to localize to the plasma membrane (Nist-Lund et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TMC4 is a voltage-dependent chloride channel that is predominantly expressed in the taste buds in the posterior region of the tongue.
source: TMC4 is a voltage-dependent chloride channel that is predominantly expressed in the taste buds in the posterior region of the tongue (Kasahara et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TMC6 and TMC8 are localized to the ER and play crucial roles in zinc transport.
source: TMC6 and TMC8 are localized to the ER and play crucial roles in zinc transport (Lazarczyk et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TMC7 deficiency resulted in complete male infertility with an OAT-like phenotype.
source: In this study, we demonstrated that Tmc7 was predominantly expressed in testes (Figure 1E), and by generating knockout mice lacking TMC7 we found that TMC7 deficiency resulted in complete male infertility with an OAT-like phenotype.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by fertility testing and phenotypic analysis.

claim: Tmc7–/–mice showed various defects, such as abnormal sperm head, disorganized mitochondrial sheaths, and reduced number of elongating spermatids.
source: Tmc7–/–mice showed various defects, such as abnormal sperm head, disorganized mitochondrial sheaths, and reduced number of elongating spermatids.
evidence: This is a summary of primary findings supported by multiple analyses in Figure 2.

claim: TMC7 colocalized with GM130, but not with TGN46.
source: Interestingly, we found that TMC7 colocalized with GM130, but not with TGN46 (Figure 4B and C), as illustrated by the immunofluorescence co-staining assay, indicating that TMC7 located on the cis side of the Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: TMC7 is located on the cis side of the Golgi apparatus.
source: Interestingly, we found that TMC7 colocalized with GM130, but not with TGN46 (Figure 4B and C), as illustrated by the immunofluorescence co-staining assay, indicating that TMC7 located on the cis side of the Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization pattern with Golgi markers.

claim: Fragmented and malformed acrosomes and proacrosomal vesicles were found to accumulate around the acrosomes in Tmc7–/– mice.
source: We observed fragmented and malformed acrosomes and proacrosomal vesicles were found to accumulate around the acrosomes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TMC7 might function as a lipid scramblase.
source: TMC7 has similar amino acid sequence and predicted structure with TMC1/2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting TMC7 might function as a lipid scramblase and an ion channel.
evidence: This is speculated based on structural similarity to TMC1/2.

claim: TMC7 might function as an ion channel.
source: TMC7 has similar amino acid sequence and predicted structure with TMC1/2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting TMC7 might function as a lipid scramblase and an ion channel.
evidence: This is speculated based on structural similarity to TMC1/2 and observed ion homeostasis defects.

claim: GM130 deficiency results in acrosome biogenesis failure and male infertility because proacrosomal vesicles are unable to fuse to form acrosomes.
source: GM130 deficiency results in acrosome biogenesis failure and male infertility because proacrosomal vesicles are unable to fuse to form acrosomes (Lazarczyk et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (note: the citation appears to be incorrect in the original text).

claim: TMC7 depletion significantly reduced the protein level of GM130.
source: Our findings showed that TMC7 was colocalized with GM130 and that TMC7 depletion significantly reduced the protein level of GM130.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data in Figure 4.

claim: GOLGA3, PICK1, and several other Golgi proteins are required for acrosome biogenesis.
source: Further, GOLGA3, PICK1, and several other Golgi proteins are also required for acrosome biogenesis (Xiong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Upon TMC7 depletion, the Golgi apparatus undergoes significant disorganization and is unable to correctly orient toward the acrosome.
source: Our findings highlight the role of TMC7 in maintaining cellular homeostasis. Upon TMC7 depletion, the Golgi apparatus undergoes significant disorganization and is unable to correctly orient toward the acrosome.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TEM and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3.

claim: TMC7 is essential for maintaining the intracellular pH and ion homeostasis.
source: The mechanism behind this is that intracellular Ca2+ concentrations decreased while the pH value was increased in Tmc7–/– germ cells compared to WT germ cells, suggesting that TMC7 is essential for maintaining the intracellular pH and ion homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed changes in Ca2+ and pH levels shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: TMC7 deficiency led to increased ROS levels, Golgi and ER stress, ultimately resulting in apoptosis of spermatids.
source: Our findings further revealed that TMC7 deficiency led to increased ROS levels, Golgi and ER stress, ultimately resulting in apoptosis of spermatids.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple findings including ROS measurements, stress marker analysis, and TUNEL assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: NHE8 is involved in the maintenance of intracellular pH and ion homeostasis.
source: The Na+/H+ exchanger NHE8 is involved in the maintenance of intracellular pH and ion homeostasis, and NHE8 deficiency leads to Golgi-derived vesicles failing to form large acrosomal granules and the acrosomal cap (Oberheide et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: NHE8 deficiency leads to Golgi-derived vesicles failing to form large acrosomal granules and the acrosomal cap.
source: The Na+/H+ exchanger NHE8 is involved in the maintenance of intracellular pH and ion homeostasis, and NHE8 deficiency leads to Golgi-derived vesicles failing to form large acrosomal granules and the acrosomal cap (Oberheide et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SLC9A3 is a Na+/H+ exchanger expressed in the acrosomal region of spermatids.
source: SLC9A3 is another Na+/H+ exchanger, and it is expressed in the acrosomal region of spermatids and loss of SLC9A3 causes severe acrosomal defects (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Loss of SLC9A3 causes severe acrosomal defects.
source: SLC9A3 is another Na+/H+ exchanger, and it is expressed in the acrosomal region of spermatids and loss of SLC9A3 causes severe acrosomal defects (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TMC7 localizes to the cis-Golgi region in spermatids and is essential for acrosome biogenesis and for male fertility.
source: In conclusion, our findings show that TMC7 localizes to the cis-Golgi region in spermatids and that this is essential for acrosome biogenesis and for male fertility.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple findings throughout the study.

claim: In the absence of TMC7, intracellular pH and ion homeostasis is disrupted.
source: In the absence of TMC7, intracellular pH and ion homeostasis is disrupted, and this leads to Golgi disorganization and failure to correctly orientate to the acrosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on flow cytometry data and Golgi morphology analysis shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Disrupted pH and ion homeostasis leads to Golgi disorganization and failure to correctly orientate to the acrosome.
source: In the absence of TMC7, intracellular pH and ion homeostasis is disrupted, and this leads to Golgi disorganization and failure to correctly orientate to the acrosome.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed correlation between ion homeostasis disruption and Golgi defects.

claim: Golgi-derived proacrosomal vesicles are unable to fuse with the developing acrosome in TMC7-deficient mice.
source: Subsequently, Golgi-derived proacrosomal vesicles are unable to fuse with the developing acrosome and acrosome biogenesis is severely impaired, and thus TMC7-deficent male mice are completely infertile.
evidence: This is inferred from TEM showing accumulated vesicles and GOPC/PNA colocalization data in Figure 3.

claim: Acrosome biogenesis is severely impaired in TMC7-deficient mice.
source: Subsequently, Golgi-derived proacrosomal vesicles are unable to fuse with the developing acrosome and acrosome biogenesis is severely impaired, and thus TMC7-deficent male mice are completely infertile.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by PNA staining and TEM data in Figure 3.

claim: TMC7-deficient male mice are completely infertile.
source: Subsequently, Golgi-derived proacrosomal vesicles are unable to fuse with the developing acrosome and acrosome biogenesis is severely impaired, and thus TMC7-deficent male mice are completely infertile.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by fertility testing data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: TMC1 deficiency leads to membrane blebbing and PS externalization at the apical region of hair cells.
source: Similarly, TMC1 deficiency leads to membrane blebbing and PS externalization at the apical region of hair cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge used for comparison.

claim: TMC1 is not only an ion channel but also a lipid scramblase.
source: TMC1 is not only an ion channel but also a lipid scramblase, which is required to maintain homeostasis in hair cells (Ballesteros and Swartz, 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TMC1 is required to maintain homeostasis in hair cells.
source: TMC1 is not only an ion channel but also a lipid scramblase, which is required to maintain homeostasis in hair cells (Ballesteros and Swartz, 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.
